title: Knapsack Problem
html:
Prerequisite knowledge: Introduction to Dynamic Programming

Introduction

Consider the following example:

[USACO07 Dec] Charm Bracelet

There are nnn distinct items and a knapsack of capacity WWW. Each item has 2 attributes, weight (wiw_{i}wi​) and value (viv_{i}vi​). You have to select a subset of items to put into the knapsack such that the total weight does not exceed the capacity WWW and the total value is maximized.

In the example above, each object has only two possible states (taken or not taken), corresponding to binary 0 and 1. Thus, this type of problem is called the "0-1 knapsack problem".

0-1 Knapsack

Explanation

In the example above, the input to the problem is the following: the weight of the ithi^{th}ith item wiw_{i}wi​, the value of the ithi^{th}ith item viv_{i}vi​, and the total capacity of the knapsack WWW.

Let fi,jf_{i, j}fi,j​ be the dynamic programming state holding the maximum total value the knapsack can carry with capacity jjj, when only the first iii items are considered.

Assuming that all states of the first i−1i-1i−1 items have been processed, what are the options for the ithi^{th}ith item?

  • When it is not put into the knapsack, the remaining capacity remains unchanged, and the total value does not change. Therefore, the maximum value in this case is fi−1,jf_{i-1, j}fi−1,j​
  • When it is put into the knapsack, the remaining capacity decreases by wiw_{i}wi​, and the total value increases by viv_{i}vi​, so the maximum value in this case is fi−1,j−wi+vif_{i-1, j-w_i} + v_ifi−1,j−wi​​+vi​

From this we can derive the dp transition equation:

fi,j=max⁡(fi−1,j,fi−1,j−wi+vi)f_{i, j} = \max(f_{i-1, j}, f_{i-1, j-w_i} + v_i)fi,j​=max(fi−1,j​,fi−1,j−wi​​+vi​)

Further, as fif_{i}fi​ is only dependent on fi−1f_{i-1}fi−1​, we can remove the first dimension. We obtain the transition rule

fj←max⁡(fj,fj−wi+vi)f_j \gets \max(f_j, f_{j-w_i}+v_i)fj​←max(fj​,fj−wi​​+vi​)

that should be executed in the decreasing order of jjj (so that fj−wif_{j-w_i}fj−wi​​ implicitly corresponds to fi−1,j−wif_{i-1,j-w_i}fi−1,j−wi​​ and not fi,j−wif_{i,j-w_i}fi,j−wi​​).

It is important to understand this transition rule, because most of the transitions for knapsack problems are derived in a similar way.

Implementation

The algorithm described can be implemented in O(nW)O(nW)O(nW) as:

for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
  for (int j = W; j >= w[i]; j--)
    f[j] = max(f[j], f[j - w[i]] + v[i]);

Again, note the order of execution. It should be strictly followed to ensure the following invariant: Right before the pair (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) is processed, fkf_kfk​ corresponds to fi,kf_{i,k}fi,k​ for k>jk > jk>j, but to fi−1,kf_{i-1,k}fi−1,k​ for k<jk < jk<j. This ensures that fj−wif_{j-w_i}fj−wi​​ is taken from the (i−1)(i-1)(i−1)-th step, rather than from the iii-th one.

Complete Knapsack

The complete knapsack model is similar to the 0-1 knapsack; the only difference from the 0-1 knapsack is that an item can be selected an unlimited number of times instead of only once.

We can refer to the idea of 0-1 knapsack to define the state: fi,jf_{i, j}fi,j​, the maximum value the knapsack can obtain using the first iii items with maximum capacity jjj.

It should be noted that although the state definition is similar to that of a 0-1 knapsack, its transition rule is different from that of a 0-1 knapsack.

Explanation

The trivial approach is, for the first iii items, to enumerate how many times each item is to be taken. This yields the following transition equation:

fi,j=max⁡k=0⌊jwi⌋(fi−1,j−k⋅wi+k⋅vi)f_{i, j} = \max\limits_{k=0}^{\left\lfloor \frac{j}{w_i} \right\rfloor}(f_{i-1, j-k\cdot w_i} + k\cdot v_i)fi,j​=k=0max⌊wi​j​⌋​(fi−1,j−k⋅wi​​+k⋅vi​)

The algorithm described can be implemented in O(nW2)O(nW^2)O(nW2) as:

for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
  for (int j = 0; j <= W; j++)
    for (int k = 0; k * w[i] <= j; k++)
      f[i][j] = max(f[i][j], f[i-1][j - k * w[i]] + k * v[i]);

At the same time, it simplifies into a "flat" equation:

fi,j=max⁡(fi−1,j,fi,j−wi+vi)f_{i, j} = \max(f_{i-1, j},f_{i, j-w_i} + v_i)fi,j​=max(fi−1,j​,fi,j−wi​​+vi​)

The reason this works is that fi,j−wif_{i, j-w_i}fi,j−wi​​ has already been updated by fi,j−2⋅wif_{i, j-2\cdot w_i}fi,j−2⋅wi​​ and so on.

Similar to the 0-1 knapsack, we can remove the first dimension to optimize the space complexity. This gives us the same transition rule as the 0-1 knapsack.

fj←max⁡(fj,fj−wi+vi)f_j \gets \max(f_j, f_{j-w_i}+v_i)fj​←max(fj​,fj−wi​​+vi​)

The rule is identical, but it must now be executed in the increasing order of jjj, which is the only difference between the two problems in this form. Going upwards, fj−wif_{j-w_i}fj−wi​​ has already been updated for item iii, so it corresponds to fi,j−wif_{i,j-w_i}fi,j−wi​​ and the item may be taken again; going downwards it would still correspond to fi−1,j−wif_{i-1,j-w_i}fi−1,j−wi​​ and each item could be taken at most once.

Implementation

The algorithm described can be implemented in O(nW)O(nW)O(nW) as:

for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
  for (int j = w[i]; j <= W; j++)
    f[j] = max(f[j], f[j - w[i]] + v[i]);

Despite having the same transition rule, the code above is incorrect for 0-1 knapsack.

Observing the code carefully, we see that for the currently processed item iii and the current state fi,jf_{i,j}fi,j​, when j⩾wij\geqslant w_{i}j⩾wi​, fi,jf_{i,j}fi,j​ will be affected by fi,j−wif_{i,j-w_{i}}fi,j−wi​​. This is equivalent to being able to put item iii into the backpack multiple times, which is consistent with the complete knapsack problem and not the 0-1 knapsack problem.

Multiple Knapsack

Multiple knapsack is also a variant of the 0-1 knapsack. The main difference is that there are kik_iki​ of each item instead of just 111.

Explanation

A very simple idea is: "choose each item kik_iki​ times" is equivalent to "kik_iki​ of the same item is selected one by one". Thus converting it to a 0-1 knapsack model, which can be described by the transition function:

fi,j=max⁡k=0ki(fi−1,j−k⋅wi+k⋅vi)f_{i, j} = \max_{k=0}^{k_i}(f_{i-1,j-k\cdot w_i} + k\cdot v_i)fi,j​=k=0maxki​​(fi−1,j−k⋅wi​​+k⋅vi​)

The time complexity of this process is O(W∑i=1nki)O(W\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}k_i)O(Wi=1∑n​ki​)

Binary Grouping Optimization

We still consider converting the multiple knapsack model into a 0-1 knapsack model for optimization. The time complexity O(Wn)O(Wn)O(Wn) can not be further optimized with the approach above, so we focus on the O(∑ki)O(\sum k_i)O(∑ki​) component.

Let Ai,jA_{i, j}Ai,j​ denote the jthj^{th}jth item split from the ithi^{th}ith item. In the trivial approach discussed above, Ai,jA_{i, j}Ai,j​ represents the same item for all j≤kij \leq k_ij≤ki​. The main reason for our low efficiency is that we are doing a lot of repetitive work. For example, consider selecting {Ai,1,Ai,2}\{A_{i, 1},A_{i, 2}\}{Ai,1​,Ai,2​}, and selecting {Ai,2,Ai,3}\{A_{i, 2}, A_{i, 3}\}{Ai,2​,Ai,3​}. These two situations are completely equivalent. Thus, optimizing the splitting method will greatly reduce the time complexity.

The grouping is made more efficient by using binary grouping.

Specifically, Ai,jA_{i, j}Ai,j​ holds 2j2^j2j individual items (j∈[0,⌊log⁡2(ki+1)⌋−1]j\in[0,\lfloor \log_2(k_i+1)\rfloor-1]j∈[0,⌊log2​(ki​+1)⌋−1]).If ki+1k_i + 1ki​+1 is not an integer power of 222, another bundle of size ki−(2⌊log⁡2(ki+1)⌋−1)k_i-(2^{\lfloor \log_2(k_i+1)\rfloor}-1)ki​−(2⌊log2​(ki​+1)⌋−1) is used to make up for it.

Through the above splitting method, it is possible to obtain any sum of ≤ki\leq k_i≤ki​ items by selecting a few Ai,jA_{i, j}Ai,j​'s. After splitting each item in the described way, it is sufficient to use the 0-1 knapsack method to solve the new formulation of the problem.

This optimization gives us a time complexity of O(W∑i=1nlog⁡ki)O(W\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\log k_i)O(Wi=1∑n​logki​).

Implementation

index = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
  int c = 1, p, h, k;
  cin >> p >> h >> k;
  while (k > c) {
    k -= c;
    list[++index].w = c * p;
    list[index].v = c * h;
    c *= 2;
  }
  list[++index].w = p * k;
  list[index].v = h * k;
}

Monotone Queue Optimization

In this optimization, we aim to convert the knapsack problem into a maximum queue one.

For convenience of description, let gx,y=fi,x⋅wi+y, gx,y′=fi−1,x⋅wi+yg_{x, y} = f_{i, x \cdot w_i + y} ,\space g'_{x, y} = f_{i-1, x \cdot w_i + y}gx,y​=fi,x⋅wi​+y​, gx,y′​=fi−1,x⋅wi​+y​. Then the transition rule can be written as:

gx,y=max⁡k=0ki(gx−k,y′+vi⋅k)g_{x, y} = \max_{k=0}^{k_i}(g'_{x-k, y} + v_i \cdot k)gx,y​=k=0maxki​​(gx−k,y′​+vi​⋅k)

Further, let Gx,y=gx,y′−vi⋅xG_{x, y} = g'_{x, y} - v_i \cdot xGx,y​=gx,y′​−vi​⋅x. Then the transition rule can be expressed as:

gx,y←max⁡k=0ki(Gx−k,y)+vi⋅xg_{x, y} \gets \max_{k=0}^{k_i}(G_{x-k, y}) + v_i \cdot xgx,y​←k=0maxki​​(Gx−k,y​)+vi​⋅x

This transforms into a classic monotone queue optimization form. Gx,yG_{x, y}Gx,y​ can be calculated in O(1)O(1)O(1), so for a fixed yyy, we can calculate gx,yg_{x, y}gx,y​ in O(⌊Wwi⌋)O(\lfloor \frac{W}{w_i} \rfloor)O(⌊wi​W​⌋) time. Therefore, the complexity of finding all gx,yg_{x, y}gx,y​ is O(⌊Wwi⌋)×O(wi)=O(W)O(\lfloor \frac{W}{w_i} \rfloor) \times O(w_i) = O(W)O(⌊wi​W​⌋)×O(wi​)=O(W). In this way, the total complexity of the algorithm is reduced to O(nW)O(nW)O(nW).

Mixed Knapsack

The mixed knapsack problem involves a combination of the three problems described above. That is, some items can only be taken once, some can be taken infinitely, and some can be taken at most kkk times.

The problem may seem daunting, but as long as you understand the core ideas of the previous knapsack problems and combine them together, you can do it. The pseudo code for the solution is as:

for (each item) {
  if (0-1 knapsack)
    Apply 0-1 knapsack code;
  else if (complete knapsack)
    Apply the complete knapsack code;
  else if (multiple knapsack)
    Apply multiple knapsack code;
}
